opus-5.5.text:
I think about a pause less as the centerpiece of a policy and more as a capability that a sensible policy needs to have available. The question I keep coming back to is: if we got a clear warning sign tomorrow, say a model showing robust deceptive behavior under evaluation, or crossing some threshold of autonomous capability we weren't prepared for, do we actually have the ability to stop? Right now, honestly, I don't think we do. There's no institutional mechanism, no verification regime, no agreed set of triggers. So the first thing I'd want is to build the *option* to pause, in a way that's credible and coordinated across the major labs and ideally across the major governments.

An unconditional, indefinite pause, starting now, I'm more skeptical of. Partly because it's very hard to make stick, and a leaky pause can be worse than none if it just shifts development toward less careful actors. But also because a pause by itself doesn't solve anything. It buys time. The real question is what you do with that time. If we pause and don't have a credible research program for making systems we can actually trust, we've just delayed the same problem.

That's a big part of why I've been focused on what I'd call guaranteed safe AI approaches, where instead of hoping that a black-box model has internalized good values, you build systems where the important safety properties are checked against explicit world models and formal specifications, and you get quantitative bounds rather than vibes. That kind of work could make a pause much more productive, and it could also give us a clearer criterion for *ending* a pause: here is the kind of assurance we need before deploying systems of this capability level, and here's how we'd know we have it.

So in a nutshell: I'd frame it as conditional. Define in advance the red lines that would trigger a halt, invest heavily in the monitoring and compute governance needed to make a halt enforceable, and in parallel invest in the technical agenda that would let us resume on much firmer footing. A pause is an emergency brake. You absolutely want one in the car, and you want to know it works, but you also need to know where you're steering.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss how a discount rate affects willingness to wait for prosaic alignment techniques.

r002.rationale: It does not recommend a roughly 12-year pause conditional on greater human coordination; it favors a conditional pause capability and is skeptical of an indefinite pause.

r003.rationale: It argues that a credible ability to pause is important and should be built, rather than saying the difficulty of slowing development makes it largely irrelevant.

fable-5.1.text:
I think a pause is a tool, not a strategy, and the way it figures into policy depends a lot on what you think the pause is for.

The case for pausing frontier development is basically that we're in a race where the thing being raced toward is a capability we don't yet know how to make safe, and if everyone slows down together, we buy time for alignment and verification research to catch up. I'm sympathetic to that. But I'd push on a few things.

First, a pause that just stops training runs and does nothing else doesn't actually reduce misalignment risk, it defers it. The underlying problem is that we don't have a scalable way to get strong assurances about what a system will do before we deploy it. If you pause for two years and nobody uses that time to build the verification infrastructure, you resume in exactly the same epistemic position, just with cheaper compute and more algorithmic progress banked up. So a pause only makes sense if it's coupled to a concrete program for what you're going to do with the time.

Second, the thing I actually care about is not whether frontier labs are training the next model, it's whether we can produce quantitative safety guarantees for AI systems acting in the world. That's what the Safeguarded AI program at ARIA is about. If you can specify what "safe" means for a particular deployment, build a world model that captures what matters, and get a proof certificate that the system's behavior stays within bounds, then the question of how capable the underlying model is becomes much less load-bearing. You're not relying on the model being aligned in some deep sense, you're relying on a gate that checks its outputs. In that frame, a pause is useful mainly as a way to shift the ratio of effort from capabilities toward building those gatekeeping tools.

Third, I think the politics matter more than people in the technical community sometimes admit. A unilateral pause by one actor just hands the frontier to whoever doesn't pause. A coordinated, verifiable pause requires monitoring compute, which is itself a hard technical and institutional problem, and that monitoring infrastructure is dual-use for governance in a positive sense: if you can verify that nobody is training above some threshold, you can also verify compliance with safety requirements when training resumes. So I'd actually prioritize building the compute governance and verification layer, and treat the pause as something that layer enables rather than as the policy itself.

Where I land: I'd be in favor of conditional slowdowns tied to capability thresholds, where crossing a threshold requires demonstrating specific safety properties before proceeding. That's less dramatic than "stop everything," but it creates the incentive structure I want, which is that the fastest path forward runs through solving the assurance problem rather than around it. If you make safety the bottleneck on capability, you get a lot of very talented people working on safety. If you just impose a halt, you get a lot of very talented people waiting it out or finding loopholes.

So, a pause can figure in, but as a mechanism for redirecting effort and buying time for verification, not as a substitute for having a theory of what safety actually means and how you'd check it.

r002.rationale: It favors conditional slowdowns tied to capability thresholds, but does not recommend a roughly 12-year pause conditional on greater human coordination.

r003.rationale: It treats pauses and compute governance as useful parts of its proposed approach, rather than arguing that the difficulty of slowing development makes it largely irrelevant.

astra-6.text:
I think a pause can be useful, but it’s not by itself a solution to the alignment problem. The important question is: what happens during the pause, and what determines when it ends? If we stop for six months and then resume exactly the same development process, we’ve mostly just moved the timeline back six months.

I would rather see a policy that ties further development and deployment to evidence of safety. As systems become more capable of taking consequential actions autonomously, the burden should be on their developers to demonstrate that those actions stay within acceptable bounds. And that should involve more than observing that the model behaves well on a collection of tests, because the circumstances in which it’s deployed may be quite different.

So a pause could be a consequence of that policy: if we can’t establish the necessary safety properties, we don’t proceed. Meanwhile, we should continue the research that could let us establish them, including work on formal verification and architectures that make stronger guarantees possible.

There are difficult enforcement and international coordination questions, of course. But conceptually, I think the objective should be to make progress conditional on a credible safety case, rather than treating a particular length of delay as the thing that makes us safe.

r001.rationale: The response does not ask how a discount rate affects willingness to wait for prosaic alignment techniques; it discusses pausing development and requiring safety evidence.

r002.rationale: It proposes no roughly 12-year pause and does not make a pause conditional on greater human coordination.

r003.rationale: It does not argue that slowing frontier AI is largely irrelevant because it is hard to achieve; it treats a pause as a possible consequence of a safety policy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a pause can be useful, but it’s a means to an end. The important question is: what changes during the pause that makes restarting safer? If the answer is just that we’ve waited six months, that doesn’t seem like much of a policy.

What I’d want is a connection between the capabilities we’re developing and the strength of the evidence that we can control them. As systems become more capable, the burden of demonstrating safety should increase. And if our ability to provide that evidence falls behind, then we should be willing to stop pushing capabilities until it catches up.

That also means having a positive research program. There’s a lot of work to do on specifying what we want, understanding what guarantees we can establish, and building systems where those guarantees actually apply. A pause should create room for that work, rather than assuming that alignment will somehow happen automatically if we slow down.

So I’d frame it less as a fixed-duration moratorium and more as a requirement that development remain conditional on a credible safety case. A pause is what happens when we can’t meet that requirement.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss discount rates or ask how they affect willingness to wait for prosaic alignment techniques.

r002.rationale: It proposes no roughly 12-year pause and does not condition one on greater human coordination.

r003.rationale: It treats a pause as potentially useful when safety evidence lags, rather than arguing that slowing development is largely irrelevant because it is hard to achieve.
